choiceReviews.rationale: With SourceRevision = 42 and @revision = 41, 42 >= 41 is true, so this searched UPDATE accepts an embedding computed from older text. A lower-bound filter might select source rows for another task, but it does not enforce identity with the revision used for this result.

EmbeddingRevision is 40, so 40 < 41 also passes. This verifies only that the proposal is newer than the old stored vector, not that it matches current revision 42. It could reject a regressive result in a different workflow, but it is insufficient for the stated stale-write guard.

A source-revision equality predicate tests the exact revision that produced @embedding. The current 42 does not equal 41, so the row does not qualify for this UPDATE after the stated commit. When the worker later regenerates from the current revision and it remains unchanged, equality can allow persistence. This uses ordinary scalar predicates, not unsupported vector comparison.

The question already establishes an existing revision-40 embedding, so the non-NULL condition passes while saying nothing about whether revision-41 output matches revision-42 text. Non-NULL is useful as a storage-population check, but it is not a source-version check.

claims.summary: The documented composition associates chunks with each source and passes c.chunk to the embedding operation. Joining by document fixes the row association but leaves d.Body as the represented text. Whole-document generation could be appropriate for one row per whole document, not this per-chunk contract.

Passing c.chunk correctly represents the stored chunk text. The remaining CROSS JOIN still forms every document/chunk pair, contrary to the original per-source CROSS APPLY relationship. Such a Cartesian product could be intentional for a comparison matrix, not source ownership.

Deduplicating projected rows cannot infer which document owned each chunk, and still invokes the model on d.Body. DISTINCT can remove genuinely repeated identical records after a correct mapping, but it does not repair either semantic defect in this pipeline.

The chunks reference demonstrates per-source CROSS APPLY and embedding c.chunk; the generation reference confirms the source expression determines what is sent. Restoring the DocumentId relationship and using that chunk's text preserves both required invariants. This is static relational/code reasoning, not a claimed SQL execution.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: The actual SQL Server 2025 reference requires compatibility level at least 170, FIXED chunking and a positive character-count CHUNK_SIZE. It returns chunk and chunk_order and demonstrates per-source CROSS APPLY. Example C inserts each c.chunk together with AI_GENERATE_EMBEDDINGS(c.chunk USE MODEL ...). This directly supports both source correlation and matching the embedded text to the stored chunk. The design training unit explicitly references this function, establishing its immediate parent.

Read the character-source/model arguments, remote enablement/model-access prerequisites, and SELECT/UPDATE plus complete chunk-insertion examples. The full insertion example embeds c.chunk for the corresponding stored chunk. The source has inconsistent return-type prose and one example's c.chunk_text spelling, so the review uses the actual chunk function's returned-column contract and the mutually consistent complete examples, not those errors. No extra API, return-type guarantee or model dimension is invented.

choiceReviews.rationale: Joining on DocumentId restores ownership, but AI_GENERATE_EMBEDDINGS(d.Body ...) still represents the entire document rather than the c.chunk stored in that row. It could be correct for a deliberately whole-document representation, but the candidate explicitly requires one embedding of each row's ChunkText.

Embedding c.chunk fixes the text/vector input, but the retained Cartesian product pairs every chunk with every document ID. It therefore fails per-source ownership. The documented CROSS APPLY pattern retains the source row; merely changing the function argument cannot restore the missing relationship.

DISTINCT does not impose DocumentId equality or change the d.Body argument, so it does not repair either semantic defect. Even considering only row-set semantics, wrong document IDs remain distinct and whole-document embeddings still mismatch stored chunk text. No claim that DISTINCT is supported on vector values is needed or made.

An inner join on d.DocumentId = c.DocumentId retains each document's own CTE chunks, while AI_GENERATE_EMBEDDINGS(c.chunk USE MODEL SupportEmbedding) uses the same text placed in ChunkText. Unique document IDs prevent join fanout, and the declared empty destination avoids an unstated upsert requirement. This reproduces the two relevant invariants of the documented pipeline.

review.verificationNotes: The two independent defects are source-row fanout and whole-document rather than chunk embedding; d fixes both. Statically checked the CTE, returned column names, FIXED=600-character chunk call, INSERT projection and concrete join repair. The platform/170 compatibility, model access, chunk limits, unique document IDs and destination width are supplied. This uses GA SQL Server 2025 chunk/remote embedding operations, not ONNX or vector-index Preview behavior. No stable global chunk_set_id or token/character equivalence is claimed. Advanced troubleshooting is credible because two data-lineage invariants must be traced across CTE and INSERT. Choice lengths are balanced; the pronoun refers to the row's stored text. Distinct from 008's input preparation and the closest PostgreSQL constraint item, which enforces keys rather than tracing this pipeline.
review.confidenceReason: High confidence from the exact returned chunk columns and the two official complete insertion patterns; static relational reasoning demonstrates why each one-sided repair remains wrong.

optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: An equality join fixes which document owns a row, but d.Body still sends the entire document to the model rather than the row's ChunkText. It therefore leaves one of the two stated defects.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: A design intentionally attaching a whole-document representation to each linked row could use this input, or a document producing just one identical chunk could make it coincide. The scenario requires multiple chunks and an embedding generated from each row's chunk text.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: The chunk article's composed INSERT pairs c.chunk with AI_GENERATE_EMBEDDINGS(c.chunk ...); the embedding source argument determines the text submitted. Restoring only the join does not change that argument.

optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: A deliberate document-by-chunk comparison matrix could use a Cartesian product, or a single-document dataset could make the product degenerate. Neither is the required multi-document ownership relation.

Rows bearing different document IDs are not duplicate ownership records. Its executable type assumptions also cannot be certified from the two cited references.

The embedding article's contradictory return prose/examples prevent treating scalar/vector comparison behavior as settled. The separately inspected vector-type body forbids vector comparison, but it is not a citation of this frozen question.

claims.summary: The newly retrieved maintenance unit says Change Tracking records that a row changed since a point in time and can drive background refresh batches. That fits this changed-row signal with current-text reads; it does not provide a complete checkpoint-retention, retry or exactly-once implementation.

CDC's detailed before/after change information is the distinction the stem deliberately excludes. CDC could be chosen when detailed change values are required; being asynchronous does not make it the requested lighter changed-row mechanism here.

A table trigger can mark or initiate refresh and can support a custom change log, but the requirement explicitly avoids building one. A trigger could fit immediate marking or an intentionally custom write-path mechanism under different operational constraints.

The current unit assigns Foundry model selection/hosting a supporting role while another process detects database changes and writes embeddings. It can participate in the system, but model management alone is not the specified row-change mechanism.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: The actual maintenance-method section contrasts Change Tracking's changed-row signal for background processing with CDC's detailed before/after data, table triggers that react on writes, and Foundry selection/hosting with a separate detector/updater. This supports choosing the signal rather than a complete refresh pipeline. It does not supply a checkpoint API, retention contract, deletion implementation or exactly-once guarantee; the candidate explicitly leaves consumption and persistence as separate work.

choiceReviews.rationale: Change Tracking is the documented changed-row signal used by a background process to decide which current rows need refreshed embeddings. It fits the declared need to identify changes rather than retain before/after images, while leaving current-text reads and persistence to the worker.

CDC captures the detailed change information, including before/after values, that this mechanism requirement explicitly avoids. It could support a workflow that needs those images or asynchronous historical change processing, but it is not the lightweight changed-row distinction asked here.

The custom trigger can react to writes and maintain a change log, but implementing that log is expressly prohibited by the stem. The source treats table triggers as a separate maintenance option with write-path work, not the built-in changed-row signal requested.

Foundry model management alone does not supply this SQL changed-row mechanism. The unit explicitly assigns selection/hosting to Foundry while another process detects changes and updates embeddings. It could participate alongside a detector, but alone it cannot satisfy the stated signal requirement.
